newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-TEEN WARS - THE NEXT GENERATION.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-TEEN WARS - THE NEXT GENERATION.

text.p: The likely shape of women's tennis for the next decade is on display on centre court at the French Open on Saturday.

The third round match will not, however, be a battle of Titans but teenagers, as world number one 16-year-old Martina Hingis and her 15-year-old rival Anna Kournikova meet for the first time as professionals.
In the late 1970s and '80s the women's game was dominated by Chris Evert and Martina Navratilova who eventually gave way to Steffi Graf and Monica Seles in the 1990s.
This year the French Open is providing the launching pad for what could prove to be the game's greatest rivalry into the next millennium.

"All the time new players are coming - it's just a matter of time," said Kournikova, whose 16th birthday on June 7 coincides with the women's final. "Monica came along when she was young and before that it was Steffi.
"There's always someone younger coming along, that's just the way it is."
Although Hingis has held the number one ranking for only a few months, the Swiss phenomenon is already looking over her shoulder at someone younger chasing her title.
Kournikova, the woman looming largest in Hingis' rear-view mirror, has yet to win a tournament but until seven months ago neither had the Swiss.

"Right now I'm number one and I'm just going to try and stay there for a while," said Hingis, who has revelled in being number one. "I don't want to give any chances to anyone to take the number one from me."
As with all great rivalries the one developing between Hingis and Kournikova possesses all the necessary ingredients, both on and off the court, to make it long and interesting.
While they play a similar style of game, away from the court they are as different as Barbra Streisand and the Spice Girls.
Aside from the fact both list Paris as their favourite city and black as their favourite colour, the two have very little in common.
Hingis, an accomplished horsewoman, enjoys her free moments riding, skiing or swimming. Kournikova prefers watching television and listening to music.

With her polished nails, waist-length honey-blonde hair and fashion model good looks, Kournikova looks as if she would be as much at home at the fashion shows of Paris as the red clay of Roland Garros.
When it comes to dealing with the demands of the media, Kournikova has more in common with moody Marcelo Rios than she does with Hingis.

Following the Russian's second round win over Italy's Sandra Cecchini, she slouched in her chair during the post-match interview, answering in the condescending tone of a pouty teenager weary of her parents' questioning.
This is in sharp contrast to Hingis, who was awarded the Prix d'Orange by tennis journalists this week as the most co-operative player on the tennis circuit.

The young Swiss even giggled off a suggestion by one inquisitor that she was getting fat, a comment that would have sent many with a typically fragile teenage psyche into a rage or running for therapy.
The two have met twice before, Hingis winning both times, including a 6-0 6-0 hammering at the U.S. Open junior championships.
"It's different now," said Kournikova, ranked 47 in the world. "It's not juniors anymore.
"Obviously we're both playing different tennis now."
"The score doesn't say anything about the match. It was actually a good match, she just won all the important points," Kournikova said.
"I don't think about the fact that she's number one. You just have to concentrate, not think about it and try your best. It's a game, anyone can win."
Hingis, however, also has the confidence of youth.
"I played her twice, I won twice. I hope the third time will be the same," said the Australian Open champion.
Before Saturday's big clash, Friday's Paris line-up features some of the more veteran stars of the women's game, including second seed Graf who plays Spain's Magui Serna.
In the battle for the men's title, top seed Pete Sampras faces a challenge from Swede Magnus Norman.
